marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q001.displayText:
Activation energy is the free-energy gap from substrate to transition state.

Activation energy is the free energy difference between the substrate and transition state.

Activation energy is defined as the minimum energy required to start a chemical reaction. Because
of the high activation energy, the rates of uncatalyzed chemical reactions are often slow. In an
enzyme-catalyzed reaction, the activation energy is reduced by forming a relatively stable
intermediate-enzyme complex. Thus, enzymes increase the rate of chemical reactions.

rationales.c: The transition-state-to-product segment describes the downhill part after the barrier, not the activation energy measured from substrate.
rationales.d: Activation energy is a defined energy difference between the substrate and transition state, not the sum of unrelated intervals.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q003.takeaway: For many biological processes, a 10°C rise approximately doubles reaction rate (Q₁₀ ≈ 2) over the suitable range.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q003.displayText:
For many biological processes, a 10°C rise approximately doubles reaction rate (Q₁₀ ≈ 2) over the suitable range.

Q10 = 2 is the correct statement regarding enzyme kinetics.

The temperature coefficient (Q10) is the factor by which the rate of a biologic process increases for
a 10°C increase in temperature. The rates of most biological processes typically double for a 10°C
rise in temperature.

Thus, Q10 (degree celsius rise) = 2 (double).
emphasis: For many biological processes, a 10°C rise approximately doubles reaction rate (Q₁₀ ≈ 2) over the suitable range

rationales.a: Q₁₀ is the rate ratio for a 10°C temperature increase and is typically above 1 for enzyme reactions; it is not fixed at 1.
rationales.c: A threefold increase is not the usual approximate temperature coefficient cited for biological processes.
rationales.d: A fourfold increase over 10°C overstates the common approximate Q₁₀ value.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q004.takeaway: Ionization changes with pH and is noncovalent; methylation, acetylation and ADP-ribosylation are covalent regulatory modifications.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q004.displayText:
Ionization changes with pH and is noncovalent; methylation, acetylation and ADP-ribosylation are covalent regulatory modifications.

Ionization is not a type of covalent modification regulating enzyme kinetics.

Regulation of enzyme kinetics can be brought about by reversible covalent modifications of the
enzyme. These include methylation, acetylation, ADP ribosylation, phosphorylation and partial
proteolysis.
emphasis: Ionization changes with pH and is noncovalent; methylation, acetylation and ADP-ribosylation are covalent regulatory modifications

rationales.a: Methylation covalently transfers a methyl group to an enzyme residue and can alter its activity.
rationales.b: Acetylation covalently adds an acetyl group and is a recognized mechanism for regulating enzyme function.
rationales.c: ADP-ribosylation covalently attaches ADP-ribose to target proteins and can regulate enzyme activity.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q006.takeaway: Catalytic efficiency is compared by kcat/Km; a larger turnover and smaller Km increase this ratio.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q006.displayText:
Catalytic efficiency is compared by kcat/Km; a larger turnover and smaller Km increase this ratio.

The catalytic efficiency of an enzyme is expressed as Kcat/Km.

Kcat is the rate constant, which is the limiting rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at saturation.
It is given by Vmax divided by number of active sites of the enzyme. Km is the
Michaelis-Menten constant, which is defined as the substrate concentration at which the initial
velocity(Vi) is half the maximum velocity (Vmax/2).

For some enzymes, when a substrate (S) binds to the active site of the enzyme (E), and forms an
enzyme-substrate complex (ES), the product is instantaneously formed. For such enzymes, the
reaction of E+S° ES becomes the rate-limiting step. Its rate is determined on the rate of diffusion
of the molecules in a solution. Hence, these enzymes are called diffusion-limited or

catalytically perfect.

Examples of the catalytically perfect enzymes, where the catalytic efficiency reaches the diffusion
limit of 108-109 M-1s-1: C
• Triosephosphate isomerase
• Carbonic anhydrase
• Acetylcholinesterase
• Adenosine deaminase wt ( >
emphasis: Catalytic efficiency is compared by kcat/Km; a larger turnover and smaller Km increase this ratio

rationales.b: Km/kcat is the inverse of the efficiency ratio, so it decreases rather than increases with better catalytic performance.
rationales.c: Ka is not the turnover constant in the specified efficiency expression; the relevant numerator is kcat.
rationales.d: Ka/Km omits the turnover constant kcat and therefore is not the standard catalytic-efficiency measure.

rationales.a: The substrate remains saturating even after doubling; lowering enzyme concentration to one-third slows the rate threefold, so time cannot stay unchanged.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q008.takeaway: Malonate resembles succinate and competes at succinate dehydrogenase’s substrate site, producing competitive inhibition.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q008.displayText:
Malonate resembles succinate and competes at succinate dehydrogenase’s substrate site, producing competitive inhibition.

Inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase reaction by malonate is an example of competitive
inhibition.
emphasis: Malonate resembles succinate and competes at succinate dehydrogenase’s substrate site, producing competitive inhibition

rationales.a: Noncompetitive inhibitors bind away from the substrate site; malonate instead competes with succinate at the active site.
rationales.b: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only enzyme–substrate complex, whereas malonate is a substrate analog that competes for free enzyme.
rationales.d: Allosteric describes regulation through a separate site; malonate’s classic mechanism is active-site competition.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 300; explanation p. 309.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q009.takeaway: Competitive inhibition can be overcome at high substrate: Vmax stays the same while apparent Km increases.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q009.displayText:

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly.to the substrate-binding site and
competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive
inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate’ concentration by which maximum velocity
can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax (maximum velocity of the reaction) istnaltered in this type
of inhibition. However, the concentration-of thé substrate required to achieve half of the
maximum velocity is increased. Therefore;Km is increased in this condition.

emphasis: Competitive inhibition can be overcome at high substrate: Vmax stays the same while apparent Km increases

rationales.a: A competitive inhibitor does not increase the attainable Vmax; enough substrate can outcompete it and recover the same maximum.
rationales.b: Vmax is not lowered in pure competitive inhibition because substrate can displace inhibitor at sufficiently high concentration.
rationales.d: Apparent Km increases, rather than decreases, because more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q010.takeaway: Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged; the statement that Km decreases is false.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q010.displayText:
Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged; the statement that Km decreases is false.

Km remains constant in noncompetitive inhibition.

Non-competitive inhibition of enzymes occurs by the binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations
different from the active site. The inhibition is not overcome by increasing the concentration of
the substrate. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction.

Non-competitive inhibtiors do not resemble the substrate. Thus, they do not interfere with the
binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, Km of the enzyme does not change.

emphasis: Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged; the statement that Km decreases is false

rationales.a: Vmax decreases in pure noncompetitive inhibition because inhibitor-bound enzyme is catalytically unavailable.
rationales.c: The inhibitor binds at a site distinct from the active site, consistent with noncompetitive inhibition.
rationales.d: In the pure noncompetitive model, substrate binding affinity is unaffected; the inhibitor reduces catalytic capacity instead.
